topic: Introduction to Topology: The Geometry of Rubber Sheets

sections.title: Prerequisites: Rigidity vs. Flexibility
lecture_lines: Geometry focuses on size, angles, and distances.
Topology ignores these, focusing on continuous deformation.
We never tear or glue objects.
animations: Display two rigid objects (cube [Asset: /scratch/pawsey1357/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/cube.svg] and sphere [Asset: /scratch/pawsey1357/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/sphere.svg]) in #FFFFFF.

sections.title: The Core Concept: Homeomorphism
lecture_lines: Two shapes are topologically equivalent if deformed smoothly.
We call this transformation a homeomorphism.
A coffee mug can become a donut.
animations: Animate the [Asset: /scratch/pawsey1357/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/donut.svg] morphing smoothly into the [Asset: /scratch/pawsey1357/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/mug.svg].

sections.title: The Topological Invariant: Holes
lecture_lines: Genus counts the number of holes.
Holes are preserved under continuous deformation.
Tearing or sealing changes the genus.
animations: Display a solid [Asset: /scratch/pawsey1357/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/donut.svg] and a circle in #FFFFFF.
Highlight the 'hole' in the circle with #FFFF00.
Label the number of holes (0 vs 1) using the [Asset: /scratch/pawsey1357/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/donut.svg] as a reference.

sections.title: Real-World Application: The Hair Ball Theorem
lecture_lines: The Hairy Ball Theorem explains global properties.
You cannot comb a sphere's fur flat.
At least one cowlick must exist.
animations: Display a vector field covering the surface of [Asset: /scratch/pawsey1357/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/sphere.svg] in #FFFFFF.
Highlight the 'bald spots' (singularities) on the [Asset: /scratch/pawsey1357/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/sphere.svg] in #FF0000.

Demonstrate the hairy ball theorem by attempting to smooth the fur on [Asset: /scratch/pawsey1357/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/cow.svg], proving the impossibility of combing hair without singularities.

sections.title: Summary and Conclusion
lecture_lines: If you don't tear, holes define objects.
Equivalent shapes are fundamentally the same.
